newsitem.title: MEXICO: Few roadblocks seen for economy in Mexico Congress.
newsitem.headline: Few roadblocks seen for economy in Mexico Congress.

text.p: Pushing important bills like the federal budget through Mexico's Congress now the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) has likely lost its majority could be easier than some have expected, economists said on Tuesday.
The newly strengthened forces of the conservative National Action Party (PAN) and the left-wing Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) could bring more scrutiny to government policies.
But all the major parties are likely to be on their best behaviour, trying to show they can govern ahead of the 2000 elections, analysts said.
"It is in the best interest of both the PAN and PRD to prove that a Congress without a PRI majority can work," said independent Mexico City economist Jonathan Heath.

While final official data is not in yet, preliminary results show the PRI has lost its outright majority in the lower house, and will instead have to have to negotiate to pass legislation in the Chamber of Deputies.
Moreover, the PRD candidate Cuauhtemoc Cardenas won the job as Mexico City's new mayor by a landslide, giving that party greater influence if not direct power.
"What is going to happen most probably is that there will be some political arrangements," said ING Barings economist Sergio Martin.
"Besides I think the government will be more inclined to discuss things with the political parties, especially with the PRD," he added.
Salomon Brothers said in a report that the main change is that the budget process will now require more lobbying, negotiation and concession than before.
"We anticipate that a resonable budget compromise can be worked out between the PRI and the opposition parties," it said."
Robert Fleming Inc economist Omar Boria said that much of the opposition to reform measures had previously come from within President Ernesto Zedillo's party itself. This could now change.
For example, the government's proposed privatization of the petrochemical industry was weakened by a PRI-led Congress.
"We believe that prospects for the approval of Zedillo's delayed agenda will improve after the political reshaping," Boria said.
Specific measures such as labor reform could draw now support from both the opposition parties rather than being solely dependent upon a fractious PRI, he noted.
"In our view, comprehensive reforms are more likely after the formation of the new Congress, next September," Boria said.
The shifting of the balance of power in the lower house of Congress could, however, bring more scrutiny to the government's economic policies.
Control of various commissions, such as the finance and budget, in the Chamber of Deputies will be up for grabs now.
So as well as throwing more light on the budgeting process, the opposition parties could use the commissions to examine institutions such as the Banco de Mexico.
"They will be calling in more people from Congress for hearings and especially from the Banco of Mexico, but also others," said Jonathan Heath.
"Congressional hearings were always allowed by Congress, and the PRD has always been in favour of the independence of the Banco de Mexico, but they have wanted to make it more accountable," he said.
Deputy Finance Minister Martin Werner told Reuters after the election that the PRI had enough seats in the lower house to enable it to forge consensus.
